title: pfind work session: finding out how much was really done

concept.big_picture:
pfind is a search tool you built for your own computer. Over the past weeks, prior sessions of work tried to make it more powerful by absorbing the capabilities of two other tools — ripgrep (fast file search) and eza (a better file listing tool). Today's session had one job: find out whether that merge was actually complete, because five different notes left by those prior sessions all said different things. One said 70% done. Another said 100% done and tested. Three others said something in between.

Today we went back to the original sources — the actual code files for ripgrep and eza — and counted every feature each tool has. Then we counted every feature pfind now has. The difference is the real answer. No guessing, no reading prior notes.

The real answer is about 80% complete. That is between the most pessimistic prior estimate (70%) and the most optimistic (100%). The 100% claim was wrong because a specific feature — glob filtering — had been added to the menus but was silently not doing anything. That bug had actually been fixed in the code, but the notes never caught up.

before_after.before: Unknown. Five notes said five different things: 70%, 85-90%, 85-90%, 100%, and 70% again.
before_after.after: Known: ~80%. About 82 features fully working, 9 partially working, 37 not yet done.

before_after.before: Five contradictory documents in the pfind folder, no single reliable reference.
before_after.after: One STATUS_REPORT.md (343 lines), explicitly marked as the single source of truth, superseding all five prior documents.
before_after.who_it_affects: any agent or person who needs to know what pfind can do

before_after.before: Documented as broken in GLOB_BUG_FINDINGS.md — the -g flag was accepted but silently ignored, so filtering by file pattern produced wrong results with no warning.
before_after.after: Confirmed fixed. The fix was already in the code before today's session. The contradiction (bug documented as open, but code already fixed) is now resolved in the STATUS_REPORT.
before_after.who_it_affects: anyone using pfind --glob to filter by file pattern

concept.honest_state: The documentation is genuinely done — STATUS_REPORT.md is verified against primary sources and is the one reliable reference. The code (pfind.py at v3.0.0) was not changed today and is not committed to git, so the version control history still shows v2.1.0 as the official version. The ~37 missing features were not implemented. No new code was written today.
concept.worst_case: The v3.0.0 code exists only in the working folder, not saved to git. If the file were accidentally deleted or overwritten before being committed, all of the merge work from prior sessions would be lost permanently. git HEAD is still the old v2.1.0 version. This is the most urgent risk — not a documentation problem but a data loss risk.

what_you_can_do_now: Read STATUS_REPORT.md in the pfind folder for a reliable, source-verified account of what pfind can and cannot do.
Trust the --glob flag: pfind --glob '*.md' will correctly return only Markdown files (the bug is fixed).
Know exactly which 37 features are still missing and in what priority order — Section 6 of STATUS_REPORT.md lists them.

what_is_still_missing.item: pfind v3.0.0 not committed to git
what_is_still_missing.practical_impact: The safety net does not exist. A file accident means losing weeks of merge work.

what_is_still_missing.item: ~37 flags from the action plan not yet implemented
what_is_still_missing.practical_impact: Features like --encoding (for non-English codebases), --time-style long-iso, --git-repos, column suppression flags (--no-permissions, --no-filesize) are absent. Most users will not miss them. Power users doing specific tasks may hit these limits.
You cannot set a default time style via TIME_STYLE or override terminal width via COLUMNS. Every preference must be passed as a flag each time.

what_is_still_missing.item: Archive search (the -z flag) does not handle zip or tar files in the Python fallback mode
what_is_still_missing.practical_impact: When ripgrep is available (which it usually is), this does not matter — ripgrep handles zip and tar. But on a machine without ripgrep, searching inside zip archives silently fails.

how_to_verify.task_title: Check that STATUS_REPORT.md reflects what pfind.py actually contains

steps.action: Open a terminal in the pfind folder and run: python3 pfind.py --help 2>&1 | grep -c '\-\-'
steps.success_looks_like: A number of 90 or higher. This confirms pfind exposes the flags STATUS_REPORT.md says are implemented.
A tree view of the pfind folder appears with Unicode connectors (├── and └──). No error messages.
A table showing Language / Files / Lines / Code / Comments / Blanks appears. pfind.py shows as Python with roughly 1969 lines.
pfind.py appears as a result with a line number showing where rrf_fuse is defined.

should_you_be_concerned: Yes, on one specific point: the v3.0.0 code is not in git. Everything else is in good shape — the documentation is accurate, the tool works, the glob bug is fixed. But weeks of merge work exist only as unsaved changes in the working folder. A git commit takes 30 seconds and eliminates that risk entirely. That is the one actionable concern from today's session.

glossary.definition: A version control system that saves snapshots of your files. 'Committing' saves the current state permanently so it can always be recovered.
The files as they exist on disk right now, before being saved to git. Changes in the working tree can be lost; changes in git cannot.
A fast file-search tool. pfind uses it internally when it is installed, falling back to slower Python code when it is not.
A file listing tool (a modern replacement for the ls command). pfind absorbed its display capabilities: tree views, permission columns, git status badges, icons.
The core ranking algorithm in pfind. It combines scores from name search, content search, and semantic search into one ranked list, so the most relevant result appears first.
A pattern for matching filenames, like *.md (all Markdown files) or *.py (all Python files). The --glob flag in pfind filters search results to only matching files.
